note: Human-reviewed list. The model never adds or edits entries; it only writes the one-sentence why. Every citation is a placeholder (verified:false) until a person checks it against the source; the UI marks it as not checked. Fitness and mind-body entries cite general public physical-activity guidelines or none; no study is invented.

entries.title: Breathe slowly for 5 minutes right before your next Muse session.
entries.how: About 6 breaths a minute: in for 4 seconds, out for 6. The Muse breathing guide can pace it, or do it on your own.

evidence.summary: Slow breathing near 6 a minute raised heart-rate variability and lowered self-rated anxiety across small studies. Effects are short-term; long-term evidence is thinner.

sources.cite: Systematic review of slow breathing, 15 studies (Zaccaro 2018)

entries.title: Read for 10 minutes before a session.
entries.how: Any book, no screens.

evidence.summary: One small unpublished test. Shown as also considered, never suggested.

sources.cite: Reading before a session, 2009 unpublished test (rated weak)

entries.title: Take a 25-minute brisk walk outside before 5 PM.
entries.how: Brisk means you can talk but not sing. Outside beats a treadmill: you get the daylight too.

evidence.summary: Regular moderate activity improves sleep quality in large reviews.

sources.cite: 2018 US Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee report

entries.title: Keep today's training easy: a walk or mobility, not intervals.
entries.how: Easy means effort under 10 on WHOOP. A hard day can wait until HRV is back near your usual.
entries.typeLabel: Easy day when HRV is low
entries.shortTitle: Easy training when HRV is under your usual

evidence.summary: Adjusting training to morning HRV gave similar or better fitness with fewer hard days in small trials.

entries.title: Decide the oldest waiting funding request before noon.
entries.how: Open Business, read the request, and decide. Amara won't decide for you.

evidence.summary: From your own ledger only. There's no outside science claim for business habits.

entries.title: Lights warm and dim after 9 PM.
entries.how: Switch the living room and bedroom to the warm evening scene yourself. Amara only suggests and checks.
entries.shortTitle: Lights warm and dim after 9 PM

evidence.summary: Bright room light in the evening delayed melatonin in a lab study; dimmer, warmer light did less.

entries.title: Do a 3-round bodyweight circuit: 10 squats, 8 push-ups, 20-second plank, 10 glute bridges.
entries.how: Rest 60 seconds between rounds. Knees-down push-ups are fine. Effort about 6 out of 10: you finish feeling you could do another round.

evidence.summary: General exercise-science consensus, backed by public physical-activity guidelines. No single study is cited.

sources.cite: US Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018)

entries.title: Run a 10-minute EMOM: on odd minutes 8 push-ups, on even minutes 12 squats.
entries.how: EMOM means every minute on the minute; the rest of each minute is your break. Stop early if form slips. Effort about 6 out of 10.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Do a 10-minute core session: 3 rounds of a 20-30 second plank, a 20-second side plank each side, and 8 dead bugs each side.
entries.how: Keep your ribs down and breathe steadily. This is a light session you can do on a tired day.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Do 3 sets of 6-8 split squats on each leg, lowering for 3 seconds.
entries.how: Hold a wall for balance if you need it. Rest 60-90 seconds between sets. Stop each set with 2 reps still in reserve.

evidence.summary: General exercise-science consensus, backed by public physical-activity guidelines. No single study is cited.

sources.cite: US Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018)

entries.title: Do 3 sets of 12 glute bridges, then 3 sets of 10 hip hinges with your hands behind your head.
entries.how: Move slowly and squeeze at the top. Keep your back flat on the hinge. Effort about 5-6 out of 10.

evidence.summary: General exercise-science consensus, backed by public physical-activity guidelines. No single study is cited.

sources.cite: US Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018)

entries.title: Do 3 sets of slow push-ups (3 seconds down) and 3 sets of 10 towel or table rows.
entries.how: Stop 1-2 reps before failure. Use an incline for the push-ups if 3-second reps break down. Skip rows if you have no safe anchor.

evidence.summary: General exercise-science consensus, backed by public physical-activity guidelines. No single study is cited.

sources.cite: US Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018)

entries.title: Do 4 sets of 10 squats with a 3-second lowering, then 2 sets of 15 calf raises.
entries.how: Rest 60 seconds between sets. Keep your heels down on the squats. Effort about 6 out of 10.

evidence.summary: General exercise-science consensus, backed by public physical-activity guidelines. No single study is cited.

sources.cite: US Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018)

entries.title: Spend 10 minutes on hip mobility: 90/90 switches, a world's-greatest-stretch each side, and a deep squat hold.
entries.how: Move within a range that feels easy. Breathe slowly, no pushing into pain.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Spend 8 minutes on your upper back and shoulders: cat-cow, thread the needle each side, open books, and wall slides.
entries.how: Do about 8 slow reps of each. Keep it comfortable; this should feel like loosening up.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Spend 6 minutes on ankles and knees: ankle rocks, calf stretch against a wall, and slow knee circles.
entries.how: About 10 slow reps each side. Useful before a walk or a run, or on a stiff day.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Stretch for 10 minutes: hamstrings, hip flexors and pigeon pose, 2 rounds of 45 seconds each side.
entries.how: Stretch to a mild pull, never sharp pain. Breathe out slowly as you settle in.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Do a 10-minute slow full-body stretch this evening, 30-45 seconds per position.
entries.how: Lights low, no phone. Work from your neck down to your calves.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Do a 6-minute neck and shoulder release: gentle neck tilts, shoulder rolls, doorway chest stretch.
entries.how: Hold each stretch 30 seconds. Keep the stretch mild; no cranking on your neck.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Lie down with your legs up on a couch for 5 minutes and breathe in for 4 seconds, out for 6.
entries.how: Aim for about 6 breaths a minute. Keep it easy; the aim is to down-shift, not to focus hard.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Roll your calves, thighs, glutes and upper back for 10 minutes, about 45 seconds per area.
entries.how: Light pressure only. Avoid rolling directly over joints or any sharp pain.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Lie down for a 10-minute body scan: relax each area from feet to head in turn.
entries.how: Eyes closed, slow breathing. If you fall asleep, that is fine.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Take an easy 15-minute walk, then stretch for 5 minutes.
entries.how: Easy means you can chat or even sing a little. No watch-checking.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Do 30 minutes of steady zone 2 cardio: a jog, bike or row at a pace where you can talk in full sentences.
entries.how: If you cannot talk, slow down. Effort about 4-5 out of 10.

evidence.summary: General exercise-science consensus, backed by public physical-activity guidelines. No single study is cited.

sources.cite: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020)

entries.title: Do 45 minutes of easy zone 2 cardio: walk-jog, bike or row, in full-sentence conversation pace.
entries.how: Take water. Effort about 4-5 out of 10. End feeling you could keep going.

evidence.summary: General exercise-science consensus, backed by public physical-activity guidelines. No single study is cited.

sources.cite: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020)

entries.title: Do 5 rounds of 3 minutes easy jogging and 2 minutes walking.
entries.how: Easy jog pace, never a sprint. Walk for the full 2 minutes even if you feel good.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Take a 10-minute easy walk after your next meal.
entries.how: Casual pace. Short walks add up, especially when you have been sitting.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Warm up for 8 minutes, then do 6 rounds of 1 minute hard (effort about 8 out of 10) and 2 minutes easy, on a bike, hill or fast walk.
entries.how: Cool down 5 minutes. Stop if you feel dizzy or unwell. Hard days are best kept to 1-2 a week.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.
evidence.risk: High-intensity work raises injury and overreach risk. Skip it if you feel ill or unusually tired.

entries.title: After a 5-minute warm-up, do 4 rounds of 20 seconds hard and 40 seconds easy for squats, push-ups, mountain climbers and high knees.
entries.how: Effort about 7-8 out of 10. Swap squat jumps for plain squats if your knees complain.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.
evidence.risk: High-intensity work raises injury and overreach risk. Skip it if you feel ill or unusually tired.

entries.title: Do 5 rounds of 2 minutes of shadow boxing or light movement drills, with 1 minute rest.
entries.how: Stay loose and light on your feet. Effort about 5-6 out of 10.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Set a 12-minute timer and repeat: 5 push-ups, 10 squats, 15 mountain climbers.
entries.how: AMRAP means as many rounds as possible, at a steady pace. Effort about 6-7 out of 10.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Push-up ladder, level 1: do 3 sets of 5 push-ups (incline is fine).
entries.how: Rest 90 seconds. Keep your body in one line. Do this level until it feels easy, then mark it done to move up.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Push-up ladder, level 2: do 3 sets of 8 push-ups.
entries.how: Rest 90 seconds. Drop to an incline for a set if form breaks.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Push-up ladder, level 3: do 4 sets of 8 push-ups.
entries.how: Rest 75 seconds between sets.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Push-up ladder, level 4: do 3 sets of 12 push-ups.
entries.how: Rest 75 seconds. Stop each set 1-2 reps short of failure.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Plank ladder, level 1: hold 3 planks of 20 seconds.
entries.how: Rest 45 seconds between holds. Squeeze your glutes; keep hips level.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Plank ladder, level 2: hold 3 planks of 30 seconds.
entries.how: Rest 45 seconds between holds.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Plank ladder, level 3: hold 3 planks of 45 seconds.
entries.how: Rest 45 seconds. End the hold when form slips.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Plank ladder, level 4: hold 3 planks of 60 seconds.
entries.how: Rest 60 seconds. Breathe steadily the whole time.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Squat ladder, level 1: do 3 sets of 15 bodyweight squats.
entries.how: Rest 60 seconds. Full range you can control.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Squat ladder, level 2: do 3 sets of 12 squats, 3 seconds down.
entries.how: Rest 60 seconds. Slow lowering is the challenge.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Squat ladder, level 3: do 3 sets of 10 squats with a 2-second pause at the bottom.
entries.how: Rest 75 seconds. Keep your heels down.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Walk briskly for 20 minutes, then spend 8 minutes on hip and upper-back mobility.
entries.how: Walk at a pace where you can talk. Move through the mobility slowly.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Do 2 rounds of 10 squats, 8 push-ups and 10 glute bridges, then walk easily for 15 minutes.
entries.how: Keep the circuit controlled, effort about 5 out of 10. The walk is a cool-down.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Do 5 minutes of planks and dead bugs, then 10 minutes of hamstring, hip and shoulder stretches.
entries.how: Everything stays easy. Finish with 5 slow breaths.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Breathe slowly for 5 minutes: in for 4 seconds, out for 6.
entries.how: Sit or lie down. About 6 breaths a minute. It is a short down-shift, not a fix for low HRV.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Take a 10-minute walk in daylight.
entries.how: Easy pace, outside if you can. Daylight early in the day helps keep your body clock steady.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Lie down for a 10-minute body scan.
entries.how: Relax each area from feet to head. If you doze off, that is fine.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.

entries.title: Spend 10 minutes on light mobility: cat-cow, hip openers, gentle twists.
entries.how: Slow and comfortable. A way to move without adding load on a low day.

evidence.summary: Common practice in coaching, with reasonable support in the training literature. The evidence is mixed in places and individual response varies.

entries.title: Start winding down 60 minutes before bed: dim lights, no hard work, a gentle stretch.
entries.how: Pick one or two: a warm shower, 5 minutes of stretching, a printed book.

evidence.summary: A common progression method used in coaching. There is little direct research on this exact format; treat it as a sensible plan, not a proven one.
